Table
Tā-b'l
n. (rendering Hebrew shulchān and lūach, and Greek trapeza, plax)
From Latin tabula, a board or plank, and thence both a writing tablet and a board for eating. English keeps both senses and so does the Authorized Version, which speaks of the tables of stone written with the finger of God and of the table of shewbread — two different Hebrew words (lūach, a tablet; shulchān, a table for food) behind one English word. The second is the theologically loaded one: shulchān derives from a root meaning to send out or spread, a table being a spread thing.

Biblical Definition

To eat at a man's table in the ancient world was to be received by him, and Scripture builds a great deal on that fact. In the tabernacle the table of shittim wood overlaid with gold (Exo 25:23) held the shewbread, the bread of the Presence, twelve loaves for twelve tribes set continually before the LORD — a standing declaration that God keeps a table and His people are represented at it. David's psalm makes the table the emblem of confident provision in danger: “Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies” (Psa 23:5) — not a table after the enemies are gone, but a meal eaten unhurried while they watch. Mephibosheth, lame on both his feet, ate continually at the king's table, which is one of the clearest Old Testament pictures of adoption. The Canaanite woman argues from the table and wins her case — the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table (Mat 15:27) — and receives what she asked. In the New Testament the table becomes the Lord's: “Ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils” (1Co 10:21), where the exclusivity is the whole point, since to eat at a table is to be in communion with the one who spreads it. Hence the Reformed practice of fencing the table, and hence the last promise: that ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.

Webster 1828 Definition

A board spread for food, and by extension the fellowship of those who eat at it; in Scripture the table of shewbread before the LORD, the table prepared in the presence of enemies, the king's table at which the lame are adopted, and the Lord's table which cannot be shared with the table of devils.

TABLE, n. 1. A flat surface or plane, of some thickness; a board or plank supported by legs, on which provisions are set for eating.

2. Fare or entertainment of provisions; as, he keeps a good table. To eat at another's table is to be received into his house and friendship.

3. A tablet; a flat surface on which anything is written or engraved. The tables of stone written with the finger of God. Exod. 31.

4. In the tabernacle, the table of shewbread, overlaid with gold, on which twelve loaves were set in order before the LORD continually. Exod. 25; Levit. 24.

5. The Lord's table; the communion table, at which the supper is administered. Ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils. 1 Cor. 10.

Key Scripture

Psalm 23:5 — "Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over."

1 Corinthians 10:21 — "Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils: ye cannot be partakers of the Lord's table, and of the table of devils."

Exodus 25:23 — "Thou shalt also make a table of shittim wood: two cubits shall be the length thereof, and a cubit the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof."

Matthew 15:27 — "And she said, Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table."

Modern Corruption

The Lord's table is made either a bare memorial meal open to anyone present or a priestly sacrifice re-offered by a celebrant, and in both cases the apostolic warning against eating unworthily is treated as an embarrassment rather than as pastoral care.

expand to see more

Rome makes the table an altar and the supper a propitiatory sacrifice offered again by a priest, with the elements changed in substance. Hebrews forecloses this: by one offering He hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified, and where remission of sins is, there is no more offering for sin. The Lutheran account keeps the body and blood in, with, and under the elements; the bare memorialist keeps only a recollection. The Reformed confession holds the middle and gives up nothing — the signs remain bread and wine, and the believer by faith truly feeds on Christ crucified, who is really and spiritually present to His people by the Spirit. The table is a means of grace, not a bare reminder and not a repeated sacrifice.

The pastoral corruption is the abandonment of fencing. Paul says that he that eateth and drinketh unworthily eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body, and that for this cause many are weak and sickly. To invite all comers indiscriminately is not hospitality but negligence, since the warning is given for the communicant's protection. Equally, to fence the table so narrowly that troubled and self-suspecting Christians are driven away is to misuse it in the other direction; the supper is for sinners who repent and believe, and the examination Paul commands is self-examination, not the elders' inquisition. The table is the Lord's, and it is guarded because it is His and because those who come to it are His.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shulchān is the table for food; lūach is the tablet of stone or wood. Greek trapeza, literally a four-footed thing, covers dining table, the Lord's table, and the moneychangers' counter; plax is the tablet.

expand to see more

Hebrew shulchān (H7979) — a table; some 71 occurrences, from the table of shewbread to Jezebel's prophets that ate at her table.

Hebrew lūach (H3871) — a tablet, board, plate; the tables of stone, and figuratively the table of the heart in Pro 3:3.

Hebrew lechem happānīm — the bread of the faces, rendered shewbread; the twelve loaves set on the table before the presence of the LORD continually.

Greek trapeza (G5132) — a table; used of the Lord's table (1Co 10:21), the tables of the moneychangers overthrown (Mat 21:12), and the daily serving of tables in Act 6:2.

Greek plax (G4109) — a flat tablet; the tables of the covenant in Heb 9:4, and the fleshy tables of the heart in 2Co 3:3.

Usage

"Of the sanctuary furniture: a table of shittim wood overlaid with pure gold (Exo 25:23-24), bearing the shewbread continually."

"Of provision, welcome, and adoption: thou preparest a table before me (Psa 23:5); Mephibosheth did eat continually at the king's table (2Sa 9:13)."

"Of communion and its exclusivity: the Lord's table and the table of devils (1Co 10:21); that ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom (Luk 22:30)."
